responses.answer:
Access on Project ADB is provisioned as a role-based bundle rather than system by system.

1. Raise the access request template through the service desk and include your learning role (Developer or Tester) and the project code ADB.
2. Your manager approves the business justification.
3. IT fulfils the bundle, which includes the repository, CI, approved tooling and non-production environments.

Once the bundle is active, complete workstation setup in this order: join the HCLTech domain and enrol in MFA, install the pinned engineering baseline from the software portal, then run the environment verification script. If a certificate error appears on the internal registry, re-import the corporate root certificate and restart your terminal - never disable TLS verification.

responses.answer:
Production data must never be copied into a non-production environment. Test environments use synthetic data generated with the approved generator and a deterministic seed, or masked client-owned data in UAT under the data owner's approval.

Key rules:
• Restricted data such as customer identity documents is handled only in approved environments, with no local copy.
• Direct production database access is prohibited; use the audited servicing tools.
• If you suspect data has been exposed, stop the activity, secure the data and report it through the security helpline within one hour. Do not investigate alone and do not delete evidence.

The production change freeze runs from the last business day of each month.

responses.answer:
Your induction follows the common foundation first, then your role-specific path.

Week one priority:
1. Complete Client & Domain so you can use the programme vocabulary in stand-up.
2. Complete Environment & Access and verify your workstation before picking up delivery work.
3. Read Application Overview to understand the five bounded contexts and the origination journey.
4. Complete Security & Guidelines - it is assessed and enforced on this project.
5. Bookmark anything you want to revisit, then attempt the quiz attached to each module.

Your learning path is six modules for Developers (four common plus two developer modules) and seven for Testers (four common plus three tester modules). Use Continue learning on your dashboard to resume the module you last opened.

responses.answer:
The ADB development lifecycle is ticket-driven and deliberately small-batch.

• Branch from develop and name the branch feature/<ticket>-<slug>, for example feature/ADB-1421-case-retry.
• Rebase onto the latest develop and force-push with lease to your own branch only. Never merge develop into a feature branch and never force-push a shared branch.
• Keep pull requests under 400 changed lines. Every pull request must reference its ticket, include tests and pass the quality gates before review.
• Reviewers check correctness, automated test coverage, security and observability. Self-approval is not permitted.
• Log your work daily in the client-mandated audit trail.

A release is cut from the release branch by the release manager. Feature branches and local machines are never used to produce a release.

responses.answer:
Testing follows the agreed pyramid and the acceptance criteria are the source of truth.

• Target roughly 70% unit, 20% integration and 10% end-to-end coverage. Domain rules and edge cases are tested at unit level; testers own component, contract and system suites.
• Use the approved synthetic data generator with a deterministic seed. Clean seeded data after each execution window so the next run is reproducible.
• A Blocked result means an environmental issue prevents execution - raise an environment defect. Never record a blocked test as failed or silently skip it.
• Severity describes impact; priority describes urgency. A core journey broken with no workaround is Critical.
• Retest a defect on the same environment and data as the original failure. Close it only when the retest passes and an evidence link is attached.
• Regression scope is risk-based and documented. Always include the smoke suite and the impacted journey; a release recommendation must state what was and was not tested.

responses.answer:
The ADB platform is organised into five bounded contexts: Customer, Product, Origination, Servicing and Posting. Each has one owning team and one published contract.

Origination is the highest-value journey. It is implemented as a saga: each step is a separate, resumable operation that can be compensated if a later step fails. When screening needs manual review, the case pauses with a structured reason code and resumes when a decision is recorded.

The Posting service is the only component permitted to write to the core ledger; no other context holds ledger credentials. The core banking host remains the system of record for balances - ADB orchestrates and posts through Posting but does not replace the host ledger.

If a change appears to affect the rules of two bounded contexts, the rule is usually in the wrong place. Raise it in design review rather than duplicating logic.

responses.answer:
Your readiness score is a weighted view of the evidence you have produced, not just the modules you have opened.

The composite combines module completion, quiz performance against the pass mark, completion of the mandatory Security & Guidelines assessment, and consistent activity across your assigned path. A score below 40 is Not ready, 40-69 is Building, 70-89 is On track and 90+ is Ready.

To move your score fastest: finish the in-progress module, attempt the quiz attached to every completed module, and clear the mandatory security assessment. Progress Tracker shows the exact factor breakdown and the next best action.

responses.answer:
I answer only from content your manager has approved and published to Project ADB. Every response runs through project and role-aware retrieval before it is written.

• Answers are paired with the module or document they were drawn from - open the Sources panel to inspect the evidence.
• I will not browse the public web, use unapproved material, or answer general questions outside your induction scope.
• If the approved content does not contain an answer, I will say so and suggest the right team to ask rather than guessing.
• Conversations are stored locally in this demo. In a production deployment they would be retained under the project's information-handling policy.

responses.answer:
Route questions to the owner of the decision, and keep the answer in the shared project channel so the next joiner can find it.

• Business terms and scope: client product owner or the product analyst.
• Data, access and environment readiness: Meridian delivery lead.
• Technical standards, reviews and quality gates: HCLTech engineering lead.
• Induction, enrollment and readiness: your learning program manager.
• Suspected security incident: the security helpline, within one hour, without self-investigating.

The weekly sync is for decisions, not for unblocking yourself. Raise blocking questions in the shared channel first.

responses.answer:
Release readiness is evidence-based and always states its residual risk.

• Every defect fix ships with a regression test that would have caught the original failure.
• The quality gate requires at least 80% unit coverage on changed code and all quality checks green.
• Regression selection is risk-based: always include the smoke suite and the impacted journey, then add suites that share a service or data with the change and the last three release suites as a baseline.
• A release is cut from the release branch by the release manager. The production change freeze runs from the last business day of each month.
• A release recommendation must state what was tested and what was not tested. An unqualified 'ready' is not acceptable.
